utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked for the witness to be kept out briefly before continuing his cross-examination. We have been informed overnight that there are some difficulties with the Albanian interpretation, entirely as a result, no doubt, entirely understandably, of the fact that Kosovo Albanians speak in a dialect that is perhaps very distinctive and different from the Albanian spoken by Albanian Albanians. We obviously have to pursue this as a potential difficulty to see how it should be resolved if it recurs, but for the present, I thought it important to alert the Chamber, and indeed the accused and the amici, to a couple of potentially significant possible translation errors. I don't know if the Court has hard copies of yesterday's transcript, but I can tell you the page numbers that I have where errors may have occurred. On line -- page 88, line 15 of his examination-in-chief, where the witness was interpreted as saying that he was happy when he saw the truck, I understand that the word "happy" may have been a mistranslation for the word "Zhur," which is in fact the town to which he was referring. So where he says he was happy, he was saying no such thing, apparently. That could obviously have an effect on the overall impact of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him in re-examination what he meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly we could do that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the accused should, of course, also know what the difficulties are. Can I just tell you the one other matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we believe to be important, potentially important? When he was asked about his injuries, at page 91, and he referred to the nature of the beating, the witness, we believe, made reference to the fact that he was attacked in the area of his kidneys - and indeed he's on dialysis now here in Holland while waiting to give evidence - but that doesn't appear at all in the transcript. But apparently he mentioned it, as we had expected that he would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matter can be looked into. The tape can be listened to, and if there are these errors, they can be put right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, is it right that the witness requires some treatment today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So we need to get through him fairly rapidly. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify one point, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, as you switched my microphone on yesterday, whether one point remained clear, and that is that I am opposed to an agreement between the Prosecution, Mr. Kay from the amici curiae, not to have the tapes shown. I am opposed to that because this is a public trial and the tapes would have to be shown. This is in the interests of justice, because no viewing of the tapes by the friends of the Court or by myself, if the public cannot see the tapes and if they are in the possession of the Prosecutor, then this does not serve justice. It is not in the interests of justice. So if the Prosecutor does indeed have some tapes which he considers supports these false accusations against me, why not have the international public see them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look at that. Mr. Kay, did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen the tapes, which is why I asked that the sound be removed from the tapes, because the sound, in my view, was prejudicial to the accused's trial. It was commentary by those who were making comments against his interests, who were not witnesses in this courtroom, and therefore that would be something that the Court should not hear. I came to the arrangement over not showing the film because there's a description of the film on the documents, and in my judgement, it wouldn't have served any purpose in relation to the evidence in the case at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is entitled to request that the films do be played in public, and obviously that's a matter we'll have to consider, which we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. He's entitled to that. Again, we would say with the proviso of no sound, as that would be in his interest, and no doubt arrangements can be made by the Court for the showing of those films at an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue which we have to determine is, of course, the necessity for evidence to be given in public as against the expeditious carrying out of the trial and whether it's necessary for every videotape to be shown in public, in this case lasting three hours, is something we'll have to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If this evidence is needed to be seen, it might be better to take perhaps a passage in the case when there's a shortage of witnesses or something happens that requires material to infill a vacant space in the court day, because it's already been exhibited by the -- by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it remains clear that I don't accept any kind of written witnesses, paper witnesses, witnesses on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's a separate issue which we're going to have to address in due course. The amici have put a brief in on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Alert to the way the Prosecution were bringing their case, we drafted a paper that Mr. Wladimiroff filed yesterday to bring the issues to the attention of the Trial Chamber of the impact of the Prosecution relying on written witness statements and to raise those issues in advance and before any order was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We -- we'll be considering those issues in due course, and in fact, we shall request a brief from the Prosecution in response to the -- to what the amici have written. It may be helpful for you to address the problems, first of all, of the Rule; and secondly, of the particular circumstances of this case, having regard to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's already in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, we will return to this written evidence in due course. We're not going to make any decisions about it today, and it may be not next week either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third point that I wanted to make is the following: I wish to comment what we just heard from the Prosecutor a moment ago, namely, the assertions that an Albanian doesn't understand the Albanian language. There is no difference in dialect which would stop a Kosovo Albanian being able to understand an Albanian from Albania. But as we're on the subject of language and linguistics, as I assume that I have the right to continue my cross-examination, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the following: If I say the following to you in Albanian, "Ne kemi ba yzmet," what am I doing? "Ne kemi ba yzmet." What am I doing when I said that? What have I done, having said that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM HAJDAR ZEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. You know, I'm in dialysis at the moment. I'm not able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will tell you. I will give you the answer. Because in Albanian, "Ne kemi ba yzmet," means I offered hospitality to somebody, I extended hospitality, I put him up in my own house, and so on and so forth, I acted as host.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is those words, in his language, in his dialect, in Albanian, that the witness used. And in translation, it was said, "I helped them," and he was referring to his relationships with the KLA. It is not a question of the difference of dialect here, but it is an intention on the part of the interpreter to mitigate, weaken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not making those sort of allegations. We will have this question looked into. We will have the tape played. Now, this witness, you've heard, is in dialysis, and therefore we should complete his evidence quickly so that he can have his treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing else to say about that. I have my own problems to deal with and my own suffering. I have nothing to say about that. I was up all night with my own problems, my own worries here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zeqiri, are you feeling fit enough to go on with your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not well at all. I'm not well at all. I'm not in a position to discuss all this. I've got my own problems and worries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zeqiri, if you can deal with some questions for ten minutes, we'll allow Mr. Milosevic to ask questions for that time. Can you manage that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Please, please. Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to have to bring this cross-examination to a close. We will note the circumstances in which it happened, and that will affect our ruling eventually on this evidence. If the witness is not well enough to continue, it's pointless to try and make him. Mr. Zeqiri, there is one question from the Bench which we would ask you to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm sorry, I can't answer any more questions at all. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zeqiri, just a short question. You said yesterday that while you were in hospital, your cousin in Germany called you and told you that your family had been killed. My question is this: How did your cousin get to know that your family had been killed?

utterances.speaker: AGIM HAJDAR ZEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had found out that the family had been killed, and I called them. I telephoned with them and I found out. That's how I found out from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did your cousin tell you how did he come to know the fact that your family had been killed?

utterances.speaker: AGIM HAJDAR ZEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the death of your family, but did you know how your family had been killed, on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: AGIM HAJDAR ZEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask. He just told me. I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zeqiri. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called by my learned friend Ms. Romano, there's an issue in relation to exhibits that arises with this witness and which will recur, I think, with other witnesses. It's to do with the potential recognition of military vehicles of one kind and another. The exhibit that we'll be asking this witness, and I think others, to look at is available to the Chamber in colour and available to the accused in colour. He may have had one served on him this morning but probably won't have looked at it. Can I hand one in to the Chamber, in any event, and one to the accused at the moment? If I'm rationing the colour copies, it's that they are limited in number. I think the amici have already had this. I hope they have. If not, I'll give it to them in black and white. But I think they have. The procedural problem or procedural issue is this: There is a key, which we trust is accurate, identifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you don't have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm asking you Chamber to share at the moment because of the limited number of colour copies and the plenty of black-and-white copies. We have a key, which I'll distribute in a second, for these vehicles, which we trust is accurate. The Judges. Can you -- and for the accused. Perhaps two for the Judges and one for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could be provided with copies, because we didn't know this was going to be produced, so we haven't got it here if we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Black and white copies, if that will do for the amici?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And a key for them as well. Obviously, if the accused were represented, it would be possible to seek from those representing him an agreement as to the accuracy of the key in what is shown in the photographs. It will, of course, speed the trial process if it can be agreed that the key is accurate. If the accused is minded to do that, then we could proceed on that basis. If not, then we'll simply produce the colour photographs to the relevant witness or witnesses and call evidence later, attaching the key references to the individual photographs. We, of course, can't contact the accused directly, and although I forecast he may not be disposed to agree matters, it will save time if he's prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or you'll have to call the necessary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or we'll have to call the necessary evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I'm sorry to take time to do it. It always seems prudent to attempt to save time where that possibility exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you've got a copy of the photographs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you've got a copy of the photographs, you're being asked if you agree that these represent the vehicles set out in the "Recognition Guide," as it's called. It's a matter for you. If you agree it, you can tell us. If you don't agree, then we'll have to call -- some evidence will have to be called about it. It's a matter entirely for you whether you agree it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say that it is -- this operation is impermissible, the operation carried out by the Prosecution having the witness removed, which was unsuccessful, and who told untruths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. We have moved on from there. We are not arguing about that now. We're arguing about these -- we are discussing these photographs. Mr. Nice, I think it's a pointless activity. You'll have to call the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, so be it. A similar issue will arise in relation to uniforms. We'll distribute the photographs of uniforms at the appropriate stage and make a guide available on the basis that we'll prove it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. If you'll call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Elshani Fehim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, can you please state your full name for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: My name is Fehim Elshani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: 26th August, 1934.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Five children, of whom three sons and two girls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, Mr. Elshani?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I am of Albanian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your profession?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Farmer for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you say "for the moment"? What did you do before?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was an accountant in Rahovec local service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you stop working as an accountant?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I couldn't do that because I supported the workers' strikes for Kosova's independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you lose your job because of that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, are you familiar with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was not involved myself with KLA. I was never engaged in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any military or train -- military training or experience?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service from 1954 to 1957 in the former Yugoslav popular army, JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I lived in my own home in a village called Nagafc in Rahovec commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, I'm going to show you a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can the witness be shown Exhibit 4, map 1. This is the municipal map of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not clear. Shall I have to move from here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You just wait there. Just wait. I will show you a map.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Can I use my glasses, please? I can't see without them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. In this map, Mr. Elshani, can you indicate to the Court where you lived, the village of Nagafc? Only if you can, Mr. Elshani.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I can do that, but these are very small letters. Seven kilometres south of Rahovec, that is Rahovec village in the vicinity of Krusha e Madhe. Unfortunately, I cannot read it. The letters are very small. The road -- I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It does not matter. We can see the map, so that's enough, and you've described where it is. Thank you. Now, would you remove the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elshani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Court the neighbouring villages? Can you name the villages around Nagafc?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: My village, Nagafc, is bordering in the south Krusa Mala, in the west with Celina village, in the north with Hoca e Vogel village, and in the east with Randobrava. This means that the village is surrounded by four villages: Krusa, Celina, Hoca e Vogel and Randobrava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they are very close to each other?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: From our village, they are about three kilometres, at the most, away. From 600 metres to three kilometres, at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, I'd like to draw your attention to the period from 1998 up to March 1999. Were there any fights between the KLA and the Serbian forces near your town?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: There were clashes around our town between forces of the KLA and Serbian forces in several areas, in several areas of our town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did the fights affect the people of Nagafc and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The result was insecurity, because every day our sense of insecurity increased and the clashes of these forces led to the population migrating from one village to another, in search of safer places for the moment. On the 17th of May, I took in the first refugees from the villages of Gecaj. This was the family of Xhafer Morina, with six members of his immediate family, as refugees in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 16th of May of which year?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: This was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate for us how many people came to your village to escape fighting in the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: About 250, according to various notes that I've had. These were people who took shelter in our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, 1999, on the day that the NATO bombing campaign started, where were you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen that day in your village?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Nothing happened in our village on that day, but we did hear from the foreign media that NATO had started operations in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you think was going to happen to you and your people after the bombing campaign started?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I supposed that the worst would happen, which indeed happened the next day, on 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, when you say "the worst," what do you mean with that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: By this I mean that the Serbian forces issued a lot of communiques, saying that if they were attacked by NATO forces, they would take revenge on the territory of Kosova, meaning on the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you fear the Serb retaliation?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I think there was no reasonable person who wasn't afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you questions about what happened on the next day, on the 25th of March. Where were you on the 25th of March, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Early in the morning on 25th of March, I was in my room and I heard a loud noise of machinery, and I supposed that this must be Serbian military equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think the sound was? Serbian equipment? And why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: This was a realisation of the Serbian threats that if we were attacked by NATO forces, we would retaliate. So we had every reason to be afraid and to think that these were Serbian forces, because they had prepared us for it and made us aware in advance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later see what the sound was?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Later we saw the source of the sound with our own eyes, and we saw the Serbian forces coming between our village and Celina, with heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what did you see?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that moment I saw on the horizon, I saw two tanks, a Praga, two military trucks, two Pinzgauers, and infantry marching after the tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, I'm going to show you what has been marked for identification as Prosecution reference number K2765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it have an exhibit number? Ms. Romano, we'll need to know what those various vehicles that were referred to by names which weren't translated are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What I have, it's four pages with photographs of military equipment, and I think that what we decided before was that we are going to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I know you're going to do that, but if you have untranslated words, it's difficult for the Chamber to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I don't have untranslated -- I'm not following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you not hear what the witness said? He referred to a Praga.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will ask him to show on the map what he referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it? What is a Praga?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will ask him later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's a matter we will bring in evidence to clarify when we show the photos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: They are photos numbered from 1 to 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like, Mr. Elshani, if you are able, to identify them. Mr. Elshani, can you look at the photos there on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you please let the witness look at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I can see them, and I can identify a Praga, which is number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just a second. Can you show him the colour photo, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be easier to identify in colour. Number 4 is a Praga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Pragas did you see?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you can assist with this. It appears counsel is not following. We are at some stage going to need to have an English description of these various vehicles. At the moment, we've got a photograph. We've got nothing on the record as to what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Ms. Romano is entirely correct. I entirely understand what she was doing and I think, if I may say so, she was doing it correctly to respect the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She wasn't doing it so that the Court could follow. So therefore, it was not correct. If she would follow and listen to what the Court is saying, we'll all get on much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm going to defend Ms. Romano because, in my respectful submission, she was behaving with complete propriety. What we laid before you this morning, in the hope that it might be admitted or agreed by the accused, was photographs of army vehicles, together with a recognition guide which indeed uses the name, number 4, "Praga." Now, it may in due course be possible for a military expert to describe that vehicle in some other way. For my part, I can't describe it. It's described by this witness and maybe others as a Praga. Praga is what it is. And what Ms. Romano is doing, and quite properly, is to ask the witness to look at photographs, to attach photographs to the descriptions with which he is familiar, and I hope that that will be a proper way and a convenient way to proceed. As the Court has correctly said, preserving the accused's right to admit nothing if he so chooses, which appears to be his approach, we will produce in evidence from an appropriate witness an account of how the names on the guide attach to the vehicles, and I'd ask that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will need, in due course, a description in English of what these various vehicles are, and perhaps you could get that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry if I didn't make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I think if we can proceed. Mr. Elshani, if we can continue and look at the photographs and identify if you can and indicate the ones you saw at that day.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Two tanks, number 6 in the photograph. I repeat: Two tanks, number 6 in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any -- any other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Two Pinzgauer, number 7. I don't see here photographs of vehicles belonging to the Serbian army. Otherwise, there were various vehicles. They were called Deutz, were used for military purposes. But unfortunately, they're not on these photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not a problem, Mr. Elshani. Just mention the name or a description of the vehicle if they're not in the photos. Mr. Elshani, do you remember any other vehicles or cars or equipment that were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Besides the vehicles that I described, I didn't see any other vehicles that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard the noise and saw the military vehicles on the hill, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that moment, I and my family and the refugees who were with me, we hurried to gather some things to take with us and, with a tractor, our concern was to flee to a safe place outside the village as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what time was it when you and your family left?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: About 6.00 in the morning. Around then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe your family?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: By "family" you mean my immediate family or my more extended family?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediate family.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: If you mean on that day, those when we fled, those who were with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: There was my son Musa Elshani; my daughter-in-law, Musa's wife, Myrvete Elshani; my wife Mereme Elshani; also Xhafer Elshani, with his family who were refugees from Gecaj; Hydajeti from Drenovci, who was also a refugee with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Elshani, apart from your family, were there other people that left with you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: All the villagers left the village at the same time and went to safer places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Well, we went -- I would like to make a correction, because I remained in the village but my family went outside the village. And I remained behind, but all my family went away with the other villagers. And here I'm correcting myself in case we get on the wrong track. And the whole village went to a village called the village -- to find a safer place, the place called The Spring of Cila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you sent your family away, and you stayed at your home?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I stayed in my own home with my two brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you send your family away?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I sent my family away for their safety, in case they were burnt or massacred, because we didn't know what would happen from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, after they left and you stayed at home, what did you -- what did you see? What did happen?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After we remained behind at home, Serbian forces -- Serbian forces moved very slowly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Serbian forces," can you be more clear what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Well, it's what I said before. Two tanks, a Praga, two Pinzgauer, two Deutz. These were the Serbian forces that came up to our village. And I described earlier that Nagafc and Celina are not more than 600 metres apart, and these forces were between the two villages. It seemed to me that -- that they were forces. How else to describe them? Of course military forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they approaching your village? Where are they coming from?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: They came from the direction of Rahovec, on a rural road which was called The Field of Paskidol, and they came along this -- this byroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see them, what they are doing? Did you see them doing or did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: As I said before, because our village is in a valley, the troops that came in our direction appeared on the horizon, and with my own eyes, from my window, I saw them, but I wasn't able to identify them. Because if you see them in a photograph, you see them on the horizon but you couldn't see their uniforms. They were about 300 or 400 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they approaching your village, the tanks and the Pragas, were they doing anything? Were they firing?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: For the moment, no. They stayed for a long time between the village of Nagafc and the village of Celina. Meanwhile, they set off towards Celina and entered Celina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do in Celina?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Gunshots from various kinds of weapons were heard from Celina, but in the meantime, Prestovc and Hoca e Vogel started burning, but you could only see the smoke and flame from them. But when they started the operation in Celina, this smoke from Celina came to our village. And of course, the burning went on and there was no stopping the gunfire, and there was a panic such as you can't describe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right now you're referring to your village. Right now you're in Nagafc. So they arrived in Nagafc, and they start shooting and burning also Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness tell the story. Let the witness tell the story. They started in Celina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then where did the Serb forces go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At about 1400 hours, they came from Celina. The same troops came to Nagafc. And we are only divided from Celina by one hill, and I could see from my home, because I have a two-storey house with a cellar, and from the second floor I saw the Praga and the tank in front, at about 2.00 in the afternoon. Until 2.00 in the afternoon, they were burning Celina, and we saw the smoke and heard the gunshots, but we haven't got a witness to say what happened in Celina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were at the house at that moment?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have anybody else with you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was with my two brothers, Ismail and Qerim. As I mentioned before, two brothers older than me. And when I saw the troops heading for Nagafc, they started to fire from the Praga, and I saw two shots that hit the roof of my neighbour. These were the first shots fired on Nagafc. And the second, and the second shell fell on my brother's house. And then the third, on the house of a neighbour. And then they started uninterrupted firing, which you couldn't follow. And at that moment, together with my two brothers, I took refuge in my cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The firing started and we couldn't see anything from the cellar where we were. We just heard the firing. But after round about one hour, the firing stopped, and I suggested to my brothers that we should go out -- we should leave the cellar, otherwise we might get burned inside, because we could see surrounding villages being burned, and we didn't expect any better for ourselves. So we got out of the cellar, and I tried to take shelter in my yard and my brothers went to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after that, when you were taking shelter in your yard?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I saw everything burning around me. I thought that my house too was in flames. I heard voices of soldiers or policemen. I wasn't able to identify them because I couldn't see them, but I heard their voices clearly, because I speak Serbian too. And I heard them talking among themselves, and I heard an officer ordering them, "Go back. Burn that house." I don't know which house they meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I stayed in the same place where I was. There was nothing I could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the other villagers? Where were the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The other villagers, together with my family, had all gone to the place called the Spring of Cilave, and there they can take refuge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to your brothers?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Nothing happened to either me or my brothers that day. But under circumstances I can't describe, they didn't enter my house, but they burned the houses round about, but my house was left untouched, accidentally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and your brothers stay outside or did you return to your house?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: To describe this event, besides the flames and the firing, we just didn't dare move. But later, the firing started and smoke started coming out of my neighbour's house. And later, we all joined together to put out the fire in the houses of our neighbours. And meanwhile, help came, and two lads, the late -- one was Musa Elshani, and they helped us to put out the fire in our neighbour's house, this fire that had been lit by Serbian forces. And the gunshots went away from our neighbourhood, further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you return to your home after that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After that, this was at about half past 4.00 in the afternoon when these two lads told us that the Serbian troops had left the village and headed towards Randobrava, on the road, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, what happened the next day, on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: That night, my brothers and I decided to stay at home, and the next day we joined the crowd gathered together. And at 3.00 in the morning, we left the home and went to our families at the Spring of Cilave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I would say that there may well have been more than 20.000, because all the villages roundabout, Krusha e Mahde, Nagafc, Hoca e Vogel, Celina, from Retia, Opterusa, Zocishte, Drenovc, Randobrava, and all these villages, they had come to this one place as the safest for the moment. And there were people from Retia as refugees there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find your family there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes, I found them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain there for?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that place of refuge - how shall we call it? - we stayed until about 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you hear or see anything from that place outside?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After 9.00, we heard gunshots from lighter weapons, on all sides. We were surrounded. We didn't know this. And panic took hold of the population, wondering what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, when you refer to "lighter weapons," can you be more specific? Can you describe what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I would say -- I've completed my military service, and I would say revolvers, rifles, automatics, Kalashnikovs. These are what are called lighter weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see where the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The shots were coming from all sides, but we later, when we had some kind of view, we saw that Serbian troops were firing into the air with automatic rifles and were waving them, and we understood from this that we were caught in -- we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the people who were shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: They weren't firing at us at the moment, but they were firing into the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the people doing that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: How to describe it? The standard uniform that the army wear, that Serbian troops wear, of the military kind, with camouflage: green, brown mixed. Camouflage. A camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, again, I'm going to show you what has been marked for identification as K2766.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And maybe we can have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document is one page and shows a number of uniforms, police and military uniforms. Mr. Elshani, you can see several photos here. Are you able to show and to tell the Court if you identify any of the photos as similar to the uniform you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Prosecution Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Uniform number 9 was the Serbian military uniform, but at the same time, police forces, meanwhile, I saw with the same kind of uniform, with the inscription "milicija," or "police," on the arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see --

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: But also number 6 -- uniform number 9 is the military uniform that I can see, and number 6 is the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw both uniforms at that time?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: That day, I only saw military uniforms, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, Mr. Elshani: When you were telling the Court about the uniforms of the people you saw shooting at the air, the photos that you saw on the board, which ones refer to that uniform? Just the one you saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Photograph number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So what did happen after that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After panic gripped the population, they didn't know what they were doing any more. We heard from Halit Gashi, a fellow villager of mine, that Zylfi Gashi, from Hoca e Vogel, had contacted a Serbian officer, and he had told him that we must set off for Prizren and go to Albania. And then there was a movement started among the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, when you say "Serbian officer," the one who told you, can you describe what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I didn't see the Serbian officer, but I was told by people who had seen him - that's Halit Gashi - that Halit Gashi told me that Zylfi Gashi had contacted the Serbian officer and -- because there were a lot of us. There were 20.000 of us there. And the army was beyond us, surrounding us. They weren't among the population, but on the other side. And I didn't see the officer at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The crowd of people set off from Prroni i Cilave and got to the road that goes from Rahovec to Prizren, and the convoy -- at the head of the convoy, when we got to the road, we saw other troops that were positioned with mortars in a state of readiness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that positioned?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: This was at the end of a little road from Prroni i Cilave to Nagafc, and it's another road from Krusa to Prizren. And when the convoy reached the road, the Serbian forces changed the direction, didn't let them -- allow them to go on to Prizren but concentrated them in Nagafc. Didn't allow them to go to Celina or Hoca e Vogel or anywhere but they concentrated all of them in our village of Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, Mr. Elshani, what you're saying is that they guide you, and they didn't allow you to go anywhere but to come back to your village?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: To make it clear, they -- otherwise they might have allowed us to go to their own villages, to Krusha e Mahde, but people had to go in the opposite direction. They might have gone to their own village of Krusha e Mahde, which is only three kilometres away, but they made us all go to Nagafc, and they put us, all of us, in Nagafc and didn't allow us to go to any other villages. So that entire population that came from other villages, they were not allowed to go to their own villages but they had to stay in Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did not allow you to go anywhere but back to your village?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Of course the Serbian troops that -- that had taken us out of that place known as Prroni i Cilave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived in Nagafc back to your village, what happened?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After we arrived in Nagafc, this entire population that had been taking shelter at Prroni i Cilave, after a time we saw a lot of smoke, because the area where we lived is not flat but has a lot of hills, and we saw a lot of smoke rising from where the population had been, and they had burnt all the tractors and equipment and possessions that had been up there. The troops did this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in Nagafc?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: On that day when they sent us to Nagafc, that was -- that was Friday, 27th of March. And we stayed in Nagafc until Friday, 2nd of April. That's one week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, Mr. Elshani, is the Muslim holiday. Did you hear anything that day, or did you see anything at that day?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, me and my brother, we had been sheltering 600 people from other villages. And that was the festival of Bajram, and we ate just what we had. And we heard some gunshots from light weapons, and people started to panic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see from where the fire was coming?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: We didn't see where the gunshots came from, but we heard them coming from the southern part of the village. But because the population were scared, they appointed four people as a kind of delegation to go to see what was happening, because the people were indeed very frightened and were in a quandary what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: My brother and I and two others went to the village bridge and then -- and then I was told that there was a massacre at Gani Gashi's house, and there was a panic at that time. And my brother and I went through the houses of another neighbourhood, watching, and when we went to the house of Ismail Gashi, Ismail Gashi's son told me that some Serbian troops had deserted and that those gunshots had not been a massacre, and so we went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you see there was not a massacre. What was that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: When we went back from the positions where he had been, we heard gunshots again, and these gunshots were in the yard of Gani Gashi. And my brother and I decided that the best thing to do would be to gather the entire population at the school, because we -- because we didn't know what would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you do that? Did you gather all the population in the school?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I didn't hear. There were only two -- there were two policemen appeared from a stream, and they said, "You don't shoot at us, and we won't shoot at you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the police appear? Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I saw the police for the first time at the house of Cerkim Gashi, near a stream, and they were policemen wearing military uniforms with the inscription "Milicija" and with red stripes, red and white stripes on their arm -- arms, and they said, "Don't shoot at us, and we won't shoot at you." And I said to the police, "Who is the -- who is the chief?" In a nearby courtyard, there were 600 or 700 people who had been brought out of their houses and looting had begun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, they said, "Don't shoot at us, and we won't shoot at you." Were you armed at the time? Was anybody in your group armed?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: None of us were armed at all. We had our hands in our pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened next?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: And this person said to me -- when he asked -- I asked him, "Who is the main one here?" the person showed with his hand and pointed out the chief one in the yard and went there -- I heard that in Krusa Mala and Celina people had got together and collected some money which they gave to the Serb troops in order to help them get to some safe place. And these refugees who were concentrated in Nagafc, they are from Krusa, some from Hoca e Vogel. They took this initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, I'll interrupt you just to come back to the point where you said that they were collecting -- all the villagers that were with you were collecting money. What were they going to do with the money?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: They thought to give this money to the Serb troops to have it easier to run away, to escape the worst evil, they thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you think that if you give money to the Serb troops, they would let you go?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Because we heard that this is -- this was what the other villages did, Celina and Krusa Mala. They did this thing. We heard from some people that they did this. I don't know how true that was. I'm not sure of that. But this was the rumour that we heard. And someone from Krusa, someone from Celina took this initiative to collect the money themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, did you end up giving the money to the troops, to the police troops?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes. The police got the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do after they got the money?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before we get there, who gave the police the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to continue to the end to explain and not interrupt me, sir, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid not. We have to understand what you're saying, and we can't understand it if you go on. Now, can you tell us who was it who gave you the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The money was given by old man Gashi from Celina, 24.000 Deutschmarks, and Milazim Krasniqi from Hoca e Vogel, 12.000 Deutschmarks they gave to the police. But not in my presence. Please get it right: I couldn't see it because I had to stay in a house. I was afraid to leave the house for two hours. Not only me but all the other people, because troops told us -- the Serb troops told us, "Stay there. If you leave the house for two hours, we will kill you." So we couldn't leave the house. But when I returned to my house, people told me, "We gave the money to the police, both of us." And I know both these two people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for half an hour and go on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, you told the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, you told the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, you told the Court that you stayed in Nagafc from Friday, March 27th until Friday, 2nd of April, so I would like to draw your attention to the night between the 1st and the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at home?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you awakened from your sleep?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was woken by two loud detonations during the night between the Thursday and Friday, at about 1.20 in the morning. At that time, I heard the gunshots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the sound that you heard?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: We heard such sound firing that my wife and I, in our bed, in half an hour we didn't dare go out of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I heard shouting from all around, from the entire village, but mostly from near in my yard, where I saw that there were gathered together the late Hysni Elshani and his family, and one was wounded in the head. And then I went to my other brother, Qerim, and there I saw Selime [phoen] Gashi, from Krusha e Madhe. And there, there was wounded Valentine, aged 9, whose leg was cut off, and who said to me, "Uncle Fehim, I cannot carry this child [as interpreted]." So I carried her and took her to the doctor, to stop the blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, the incident you are referring to, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: On Friday, 2nd of April, 1999, at 1.20 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were at home at that time?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asleep?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after? You said you woke up with a sound.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I was woken up by two detonations, one after another, very powerful ones, and they woke me from my sleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, first you said you heard gunfire. Now you said you heard detonations. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: This was the detonation of some explosive material. It was a powerful explosion, as if from an airplane. It was a blast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do after you heard this blast?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: As I said before --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'm not having translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the translation, please.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I couldn't leave my room, because everything was shattering in my room: the windows, every glass, every piece of glass that was in my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Then I left my home and I heard noises, loud noises from everywhere. I told you: For the moment, I saw the mother, the sister, the sister-in-law, Fushnaja, who had come near him, and were very sad because he was gravely wounded, injured. They were crying over his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At this moment, in my yard, I saw seven dead bodies and many other injured. I saw with my own eyes. But in my brother's home, there were also two other dead people, and six members of my brother's family were injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know -- do you know what caused the death or what caused them to be injured?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: From that powerful blast, I told you earlier, which inflicted many injured and dead people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did it do to the injured -- what happened to the injured people?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Even though their number was great, with great difficulties, I managed to find a car, a vehicle, and loaded on top of it seven injured people, sometime between 3.00 in the morning, and I drove them to Prizren hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what caused the detonation, what caused the blast? Did you see where this came from?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The cause of the blast, in my mind, was - and I don't think there is any need for comment - that as I said, they herded together a large number of people in a small village, over 20.000 people. The aim of the Serbs was clear beforehand; they wanted to commit genocide, to exterminate the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani --

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just -- I know that was in your mind, but I wanted to know what you saw, what you hear at that time. Did you see what caused the -- what caused the blast?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The blast came from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I couldn't see it because I was sleeping. But it is well known, and it is well known that in there were 20.000 people, sheltering in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just deal with what you saw or heard yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, you were at home at that time. You were inside your home. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I have sworn to say only what I saw and what I have experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Elshani. So you heard a blast. That's what you said. It's correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes. Not one but two explosions I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't -- did you see what caused the blast? Did you see where the blast come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has dealt with this subject. I mean, he's given various descriptions, and I have no need to say any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's right. The witness has given the best account he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just -- Your Honour, if you permit, I just want to just propose one more question that's the final one to just make it very clear as we were saying what he saw and he heard. So I just want to ask the witness if he did see or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: One question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, where you were in the house and after you heard the blast, did you see anything? Did you see where the blast came from?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I saw the traces left behind by the explosion, but actual explosion I didn't say -- I didn't see because I was asleep, but I saw the effects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of traces did you see?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I have to describe it. In my yard, there were holes from 30 centimetres to 1 metre deep. Not just in one place but throughout the yard and in the yards of my brothers too. So it was as if my yard had been ploughed up by shells. And these shells also killed these people, and they wounded people. So for -- these shells killed people, and I am a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, did you see anything else or just the craters, just the holes?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Besides the craters, there were seven dead people in my yard, two in my brother's. So nine dead people in two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elshani. After you took some people to the hospital, did you come back to your town? Did you come back to Nagafc?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After I took the wounded to the hospital where -- and unfortunately, my brother's nephew died, and they placed him in the morgue. Then I returned back to Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you came back to Nagafc?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Shortly before we arrived at Nagafc, when we got to Krusha e Mahde, I found the crowd of people who had set off fleeing, leaving the village for Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I remained in Krusha e Mahde and tried to -- and tried to organise the bringing -- the wounded to be brought to Prizren, but at that point, the car I had obtained was taken from me and I was stuck without a car, and I was stuck in Krusha e Mahde. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, who did take your car?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: It wasn't my car. I took it from somebody from Krusha e Mahde to take the wounded to the hospital. And when I returned to Krusa, he took his own car back and I was left without a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you came back to Nagafc, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I took my wife and went back to Nagafc, and when I returned to Nagafc and then I saw seven dead people in my yard and two dead people in my brother's yard, and the bodies had been left unburied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go back to your house?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was the situation at that time in Nagafc? It was calm; it was safe?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: There was no kind of security at all. But when I returned to my home, there was the family of Ukshin Hoti, the father, mother, in my cellar, and I found them there. And they had left behind because they were ill, and they were unable to flee. I also found a woman in my brother's house, and she, too, was ill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, during all the time, did you see again any police or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At about 10.00 in the morning, sometime between 9.00 and 10.00, I heard a noise, and I went up my brother's stairs, and I saw two tanks coming from Rahovec, and they entered the village. Then the noise came up to my house, and then I -- my wife and I took shelter in the cellar for security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you took shelter in your basement, in your cellar?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: We couldn't see anything after we went into the cellar, but we heard gunshots for about half an hour. And after half an hour, we heard -- we heard some noise above our cellar. And people came into our cellar where the parents of Ukshin Hoti were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of people? Can you describe who came?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that moment when they entered the cellar, I couldn't see them because I was in a separate part of the cellar. But they talked to Ukshin Hoti's father and asked whose this house -- who this house belonged to and where the head of the house was, and they said that this is Fehim Elshani's house and he had gone out to look after his livestock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which language they were speaking?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: They were speaking Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I understand Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I wasn't really able to identify the conversation, but one of them came -- they came out of the cellar where these two were. And meanwhile, the other one who was in the cellar last came out. And when he -- and when he went, I went out with my wife too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, at that point, could you see them?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: You mean those people who were in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The people who entered the cellar.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: The second group that came in the cellar, the first one, there was a tall, thin person with a bandanna around his head, and he entered the cellar where everything was destroyed. And when he saw five of us in there, he started insulting us in Serbian, saying, "Fuck your Albanian mothers. Now I will cut your throats like sheep."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, do you remember how this person -- what kind of clothes this person was wearing?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: This person was wearing a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell what colour?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Camouflage, green and brown, like the Serbian police wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do after?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: After all these insults, he took the knife from his belt and came up to massacre me, starting with me and going on to the others, all of them: my wife, Mereme, Ukshin's sister, mother, and father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Perhaps every disaster there are exceptions, because nothing worse happened to us, and at that moment there was a band of police entered the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you safe? Why nothing happened to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that moment, when he was near me with the knife, the other policeman came to the door and called him by name, and called to me, saying, "Uncle Fehim, do you know me?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I, at that moment, didn't recognise him, but he asked me, "Did you work with Gordana and Tika?" And I said yes. And then he said, "I am one of them." And then he said to me, "I recognise you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what language was he talking to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: He was speaking in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Another one came in, a policeman, and he too said to me - he called me Uncle Fehim - "Do you know me?" I answered him, "Yes, I recognise you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after -- did they do anything to you? What happened to you after that, Mr. Elshani?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Seeing this policeman that had come up to me with a knife, he then withdrew and put his knife back in his belt, and the three left the cellar together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave the cellar as well?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I remained in the cellar, and then another policeman came and took me out of the cellar to identify the victims who were in my yard and in my brother's yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: He said, regarding these victims, "You asked for NATO and now look what NATO has done." And I could only identify two of these victims, not the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police officer say anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Then I acted as their interpreter. They were asked details about the people who were left in the village, the sick woman in my brother's house, and there was also a sick old man in a neighbour's house, and they wanted me to communicate with them to get their personal details, and they used me as an interpreter to gather this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, did there come a time when you left Nagafc?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Meanwhile, on this critical day - this is Friday, 2nd of April - I had Serbian troops in my yard, in coats and in uniforms, and they filmed the corpses and the damage. And among them there was someone from the state security called Agim Isaku, and he later said to me, "You had better get out of here, because otherwise, if you're found here tomorrow, you will be in for it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, how did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I knew this person from before, because he comes from this municipality, and he used to work in state security in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing --

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: He is a Roman Gypsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: No. He was wearing plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he said to you to leave. Why did he say this to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: No doubt he knew that the next day would be worse than that day, and for that reason, he told me to leave my village, for the sake of my own safety and of the other people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave your village?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: On the next day, I took a tractor. I loaded on it some clothes, my wife, and then we set out for Krusha e Madhe. I took also the mother, the father -- I left -- sorry. I left in my home the father, the sister, and the mother of Ukshin Hoti, and then we all went to Prizren, that is, on the 3rd of April. It was Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Prizren, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: In Prizren, I stayed at a brother-in-law of mine for two weeks, because I had to take care of the injured and bury the late Hysni, because I left him in the hospital, in the morgue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, did you go -- did you walk during all this time? How did you go to Prizren and then further on?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: No. I said I took -- I borrowed a tractor and I put some clothes, some covers and coverlets, because we don't know where we would go. Some basic things. And then by tractor I went to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see more people along the way?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone along the way, with the exception of some police troops that were moving. I didn't see anyone else. No one. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Prizren, did you go to where? Where did you go after Prizren?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: From Prizren, after the injured were released from hospital, I took all of them. I mounted them on my tractor and then I drove them to Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Elshani, before crossing the border with Albania, what happened?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: Before we crossed the border to Albania -- the distance from Prizren to the Albanian border is over 15 kilometres, and somewhere around the seventh or eighth kilometre from Prizren, in the vicinity of Zhur village, two soldiers appeared on the road. They stopped me. I was driving the tractor with the injured people and the people who were accompanying the injured people. And they asked me, "Bring out all the money you have in your pocket."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: They were dressed in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened after that? Did you continue?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: I told them, "I don't have any money, because we are coming from the hospital, and I'm carrying some injured people. We are going to Albania." They let me continue on my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: When I -- when we arrived in Zhur village, we saw a policeman and a soldier there. They stopped me. They asked me to show them my passport. I showed it to them. Then the police told me, "Go on. Continue your trip to Albania," but warned me not to move outside the main road, the asphalt road, because all the ground was planted with mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He asked to see your document. Did you have to give the document as well?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM ELSHANI
utterances.text: At that moment, they did not take my identity card away. They returned it back to me. And then I continued the trip to Vermica, to the border.
